claim: Slc38a5 mRNA levels were consistently down-regulated in Lrp5−/− retinas from postnatal day (P) 5 through P17, compared with age-matched wild type (WT) controls.
source: We found that the mRNA levels of Slc38a5 were consistently down-regulated in both Lrp5−/− and Ndpy/− retinas lacking Wnt signaling from postnatal day (P) 5 through P17, compared with their age-matched wild type (WT) controls (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR measurements shown in Figure 1A and B, demonstrating decreased Slc38a5 mRNA in Lrp5−/− retinas across multiple developmental timepoints.

claim: Slc38a5 mRNA levels were consistently down-regulated in Ndpy/− retinas from postnatal day (P) 5 through P17, compared with age-matched wild type (WT) controls.
source: We found that the mRNA levels of Slc38a5 were consistently down-regulated in both Lrp5−/− and Ndpy/− retinas lacking Wnt signaling from postnatal day (P) 5 through P17, compared with their age-matched wild type (WT) controls (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR measurements shown in Figure 1A and B, demonstrating decreased Slc38a5 mRNA in Ndpy/− retinas across multiple developmental timepoints.

claim: There was ~40-fold enrichment of Slc38a5 mRNA level in retinal blood vessels compared with that in the whole retinas in WT mice.
source: There was ~40-fold enrichment of Slc38a5 mRNA level in retinal blood vessels compared with that in the whole retinas in WT mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR analysis of laser capture microdissected retinal blood vessels compared to whole retina samples, as shown in Figure 1C.

claim: SLC38A5 colocalizes with isolectin B4 in retinal blood vessel endothelium.
source: Localization of SLC38A5 in retinal blood vessel endothelium is also demonstrated by immunohistochemistry showing colocalization of SLC38A5 with isolectin B4, a marker of vascular endothelium (Figure 1D).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry images in Figure 1D showing overlap of SLC38A5 antibody staining with isolectin B4-positive blood vessels.

claim: Slc38a5 mRNA levels were substantially down-regulated in both Lrp5−/− and Ndpy/− LCM-isolated retinal vessels compared with their respective WT control blood vessels.
source: Moreover, Slc38a5 mRNA levels were substantially down-regulated in both Lrp5−/− and Ndpy/− LCM-isolated retinal vessels compared with their respective WT control blood vessels (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR analysis of laser capture microdissected blood vessels from mutant and control retinas, as shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Protein levels of Slc38a5 were significantly decreased in P17 Lrp5−/− retinas versus WT control retinas.
source: Protein levels of Slc38a5 were also significantly decreased in both P17 Lrp5−/− and Ndpy/− retinas versus their respective WT control retinas, with more substantial reduction in Ndpy/− retinas by ~50% (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 1F and quantified in Figure 1G.

claim: Protein levels of Slc38a5 were significantly decreased in P17 Ndpy/− retinas versus WT control retinas by ~50%.
source: Protein levels of Slc38a5 were also significantly decreased in both P17 Lrp5−/− and Ndpy/− retinas versus their respective WT control retinas, with more substantial reduction in Ndpy/− retinas by ~50% (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 1F and quantified in Figure 1G, showing approximately 50% reduction in Ndpy/− retinas.

claim: Slc38a5 is mainly expressed in vascular endothelium in P14 C57B6 mouse retinas.
source: Slc38a5 expression in retinal cells was further analyzed in single-cell transcriptome datasets of P14 C57B6 mouse retinas (Macosko et al., 2015), where Slc38a5 is found mainly expressed in vascular endothelium, similar as endothelium marker Pecam1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by single-cell transcriptome analysis from published dataset (Macosko et al., 2015) showing Slc38a5 expression pattern similar to endothelial marker Pecam1.

claim: SLC38A5 is mainly expressed in vascular endothelium in human retina.
source: In a human retinal single-cell dataset - Cell atlas of the human fovea and peripheral retina (Yan et al., 2020), SLC38A5 is also mainly expressed in vascular endothelium, just like PECAM1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by single-cell transcriptome analysis from published human retinal dataset (Yan et al., 2020) showing SLC38A5 expression pattern similar to endothelial marker PECAM1.

claim: Slc38a5 mRNA levels were substantially induced by Norrin by ~1.6-fold in HRMECs.
source: We found that Slc38a5 mRNA and protein levels were substantially induced by Norrin by ~1.6-fold (Figure 2A and B), whereas subsequent treatment with XAV939 reversed the Norrin-induced SLC38A5 upregulation in HRMECs (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Demonstrated by RT-qPCR and Western blot analysis of HRMECs treated with recombinant Norrin, as shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: XAV939 treatment reversed the Norrin-induced SLC38A5 upregulation in HRMECs.
source: We found that Slc38a5 mRNA and protein levels were substantially induced by Norrin by ~1.6-fold (Figure 2A and B), whereas subsequent treatment with XAV939 reversed the Norrin-induced SLC38A5 upregulation in HRMECs (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Demonstrated by RT-qPCR and Western blot analysis showing that XAV939, a Wnt inhibitor, blocks Norrin-induced SLC38A5 increase, as shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Wnt3a-conditioned medium induced upregulation of SLC38A5 by ~4-fold in mRNA levels in HRMECs.
source: Moreover, Wnt3a-conditioned medium (Wnt3a-CM) induced an even more potent upregulation of SLC38A5 by ~4-fold in mRNA levels and ~10-fold in protein levels (Figure 2A and C), which were also reversed by XAV939 treatment (Figure 2A and C).
evidence: Demonstrated by RT-qPCR analysis of HRMECs treated with Wnt3a-conditioned medium, as shown in Figure 2A and C.

claim: Wnt3a-conditioned medium induced upregulation of SLC38A5 by ~10-fold in protein levels in HRMECs.
source: Moreover, Wnt3a-conditioned medium (Wnt3a-CM) induced an even more potent upregulation of SLC38A5 by ~4-fold in mRNA levels and ~10-fold in protein levels (Figure 2A and C), which were also reversed by XAV939 treatment (Figure 2A and C).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis of HRMECs treated with Wnt3a-conditioned medium, as shown in Figure 2A and C.

claim: XAV939 treatment reversed the Wnt3a-CM-induced SLC38A5 upregulation in HRMECs.
source: Moreover, Wnt3a-conditioned medium (Wnt3a-CM) induced an even more potent upregulation of SLC38A5 by ~4-fold in mRNA levels and ~10-fold in protein levels (Figure 2A and C), which were also reversed by XAV939 treatment (Figure 2A and C).
evidence: Demonstrated by RT-qPCR and Western blot analysis showing that XAV939 blocks Wnt3a-CM-induced SLC38A5 increase, as shown in Figure 2A and C.

claim: Three SLC38A5 promoter regions (P1, P2, and P3) containing putative TCF-binding motifs showed significant increase in luciferase activity when co-transfected with active β-catenin.
source: All three luciferase reporter-containing promotor regions: P1, P2, and P3, showed significant increase in luciferase activity when co-transfected with active β-catenin, with both P1 and P2 showing ~threefold increase and P3 showing ~twofold increase (Figure 2D).
evidence: Demonstrated by dual-luciferase reporter assays in HEK293T cells showing increased luciferase activity with active β-catenin co-transfection, as shown in Figure 2D.

claim: SLC38A5 transcription is regulated by Wnt signaling via β-catenin binding to TCF-binding sites on its promoter regions.
source: Together, these results suggest that SLC38A5 transcription is a downstream gene regulated by Wnt signaling via β-catenin binding to potentially multiple TCF-binding sites on its promoter regions, either directly or through an indirect secondary mechanisms via another Wnt responsive gene.
evidence: Inferred from luciferase reporter assays showing β-catenin-dependent activation of SLC38A5 promoter regions containing TCF-binding motifs, combined with Wnt ligand treatment experiments.

claim: Treatment with si-Slc38a5 resulted in substantial reduction of Slc38a5 mRNA levels by ~70% compared with si-Ctrl injected eyes.
source: Treatment with siRNA resulted in substantial reduction of Slc38a5 mRNA levels by ~70% (n=3/group, p≤0.01, Figure 3A) and protein levels by ~70% (n=3/group, p≤0.05, Figure 3B) compared with contralateral si-Ctrl injected eyes at 3 days postinjection.
evidence: Demonstrated by RT-qPCR analysis of retinas 3 days after intravitreal siRNA injection, as shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Treatment with si-Slc38a5 resulted in substantial reduction of Slc38a5 protein levels by ~70% compared with si-Ctrl injected eyes.
source: Treatment with siRNA resulted in substantial reduction of Slc38a5 mRNA levels by ~70% (n=3/group, p≤0.01, Figure 3A) and protein levels by ~70% (n=3/group, p≤0.05, Figure 3B) compared with contralateral si-Ctrl injected eyes at 3 days postinjection.
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis of retinas 3 days after intravitreal siRNA injection, as shown in Figure 3B.

claim: si-Slc38a5 treated retinas showed significant (~20%) delay of superficial vascular coverage at P7 compared with si-Ctrl injection.
source: Moreover, si-Slc38a5 treated retinas showed significant (~20%) delay of superficial vascular coverage in the retinas at P7, 3 days after injection at P4, compared with si-Ctrl injection (n=9/group, p≤0.05, Figure 3C).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification of vascularized area in flat-mounted retinas stained with isolectin B4, as shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The development of deep retinal vascular layer was substantially impaired with almost 40% reduction in deep layer vascular area at P10 after si-Slc38a5 injection.
source: In addition, the development of deep retinal vascular layer was also substantially impaired with almost 40% reduction in deep layer vascular area at P10, 3 days after siRNA were injected at P7 (n=11/group, p≤0.01, Figure 3D).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification of deep layer vascular area in flat-mounted retinas, as shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Retinal blood vessel development was substantially delayed in Slc38a5−/− retinas for superficial vascular layer at P5.
source: Retinal blood vessel development was substantially delayed in Slc38a5−/− retinas for superficial vascular layer at P5 (n=8–11/group, p≤0.01, Figure 3E) and deep vascular layer at P10 (n=12–13/group, p≤0.01, Figure 3F).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification of vascularized area in Slc38a5−/− retinas compared to WT littermates, as shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Retinal blood vessel development was substantially delayed in Slc38a5−/− retinas for deep vascular layer at P10.
source: Retinal blood vessel development was substantially delayed in Slc38a5−/− retinas for superficial vascular layer at P5 (n=8–11/group, p≤0.01, Figure 3E) and deep vascular layer at P10 (n=12–13/group, p≤0.01, Figure 3F).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification of vascularized area in Slc38a5−/− retinas compared to WT littermates, as shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The delayed vascular development in Slc38a5−/− mice is resolved in adult mice when the retinal vasculature is largely normal.
source: The delayed vascular development, however, is resolved in adult Slc38a5−/− mice when the retinal vasculature is largely normal in both superficial and deep layers (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) with comparable vessel density in vascular coverage and numbers of branches and junctions (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by imaging and quantification of adult Slc38a5−/− retinal vasculature showing normal structure and density, as shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: Slc38a5 mRNA expression was significantly suppressed during the vaso-obliteration phase of OIR between P8 and P12.
source: We found that Slc38a5 mRNA expression was significantly suppressed during the vaso-obliteration phase between P8 and P12, and up-regulated during the vaso-proliferative phase of OIR between P14 and P17, compared with age-matched room air control mice (Figure 4A).
evidence: Demonstrated by RT-qPCR analysis of OIR retinas at different timepoints compared to normoxic controls, as shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Slc38a5 mRNA expression was up-regulated during the vaso-proliferative phase of OIR between P14 and P17.
source: We found that Slc38a5 mRNA expression was significantly suppressed during the vaso-obliteration phase between P8 and P12, and up-regulated during the vaso-proliferative phase of OIR between P14 and P17, compared with age-matched room air control mice (Figure 4A).
evidence: Demonstrated by RT-qPCR analysis of OIR retinas at different timepoints compared to normoxic controls, as shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In pathological neovessels from P17 OIR retinas, Slc38a5 mRNA levels were enriched at ~2.5-fold compared with age-matched normoxic vessels.
source: In pathological neovessels from P17 OIR retinas, Slc38a5 mRNA levels were enriched at ~2.5-fold, compared with the levels in age-matched normoxic vessels (Figure 4B).
evidence: Demonstrated by RT-qPCR analysis of laser capture microdissected pathological neovessels from OIR retinas compared to normal vessels, as shown in Figure 4B.

claim: SLC38A5 protein levels were increased at P17 OIR whole retinas by ~fourfold compared with age-matched normoxic retinas.
source: Moreover, SLC38A5 protein levels were also increased at P17 OIR whole retinas by ~fourfold compared with age-matched normoxic retinas in Western blot (Figure 4C).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis and densitometry quantification of OIR retinas compared to normoxic controls, as shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Slc38a5−/− mice showed significantly decreased levels of pathological neovascularization at P17 by ~25% compared with WT littermate controls in OIR.
source: Slc38a5−/− mice showed significantly decreased levels of pathological neovascularization at P17 by ~25% compared with WT littermate controls (n=20/group, p≤0.01, Figure 4D), whereas the vaso-obliterated retinal areas were comparable at both P17 (Figure 4D) and P12 (n=10–12/group, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification of pathological neovascularization in flat-mounted OIR retinas from Slc38a5−/− and WT mice, as shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The vaso-obliterated retinal areas were comparable between Slc38a5−/− and WT mice at P17 in OIR.
source: Slc38a5−/− mice showed significantly decreased levels of pathological neovascularization at P17 by ~25% compared with WT littermate controls (n=20/group, p≤0.01, Figure 4D), whereas the vaso-obliterated retinal areas were comparable at both P17 (Figure 4D) and P12 (n=10–12/group, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification of vaso-obliterated areas in OIR retinas showing no significant difference between genotypes, as shown in Figure 4D.

claim: SLC38A5 siRNA effectively suppressed SLC38A5 mRNA expression by more than 80% in HRMECs.
source: Compared with negative control siRNA (si-Ctrl), SLC38A5 siRNA (si-SLC38A5) effectively suppressed SLC38A5 mRNA expression by more than 80% (p≤0.01, Figure 5A), and protein level by ~50% (p≤0.05, Figure 5B), confirming successful inhibition.
evidence: Demonstrated by RT-qPCR analysis of HRMECs transfected with si-SLC38A5 compared to si-Ctrl, as shown in Figure 5A.

claim: SLC38A5 siRNA suppressed SLC38A5 protein level by ~50% in HRMECs.
source: Compared with negative control siRNA (si-Ctrl), SLC38A5 siRNA (si-SLC38A5) effectively suppressed SLC38A5 mRNA expression by more than 80% (p≤0.01, Figure 5A), and protein level by ~50% (p≤0.05, Figure 5B), confirming successful inhibition.
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis of HRMECs transfected with si-SLC38A5 compared to si-Ctrl, as shown in Figure 5B.

claim: HRMEC metabolic activity was significantly decreased at 48 and 72 hr after transfection with si-SLC38A5 (~30% reduction at 72 hr) compared with si-Ctrl-treated HRMECs.
source: HRMEC metabolic activity was significantly decreased at 48 and 72 hr after transfected with si-SLC38A5 (~30% reduction at 72 hr), compared with si-Ctrl-treated HRMECs (p≤0.01, Figure 5C), indicative of decreased cell viability and/or proliferation.
evidence: Demonstrated by MTT cellular metabolic activity assay measuring NAD(P)H-dependent oxidoreductase activities at multiple timepoints, as shown in Figure 5C.

claim: si-SLC38A5 substantially suppressed HRMEC migration.
source: In addition, si-SLC38A5 substantially suppressed HRMEC migration (p≤0.05, Figure 5D) and tubular formation, resulting in ~35% reduction in total vessel length (Figure 5E).
evidence: Demonstrated by scratch wound migration assay showing reduced migrated areas in si-SLC38A5-treated HRMECs, as shown in Figure 5D.

claim: si-SLC38A5 suppressed HRMEC tubular formation, resulting in ~35% reduction in total vessel length.
source: In addition, si-SLC38A5 substantially suppressed HRMEC migration (p≤0.05, Figure 5D) and tubular formation, resulting in ~35% reduction in total vessel length (Figure 5E).
evidence: Demonstrated by tubular formation assay on Matrigel showing reduced vessel length in si-SLC38A5-treated HRMECs, as shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Suppression of SLC38A5 with si-SLC38A5 resulted in ~25% decrease in the amount of intracellular glutamine in HRMECs compared with si-Ctrl treatment.
source: Suppression of SLC38A5 with si-SLC38A5 resulted in ~25% decrease in the amount of intracellular glutamine measured by bioluminescence and then titrated to a standard concentration curve, compared with si-Ctrl treatment (p≤0.01, Figure 6A).
evidence: Demonstrated by glutamine/glutamate uptake bioluminescent assay measuring intracellular glutamine levels in HRMECs, as shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Culture medium collected from si-SLC38A5-treated HRMECs shows a reciprocal ~25% higher levels of glutamine content than si-Ctrl-treated cells.
source: Conversely, measurement of corresponding cell culture medium collected from si-SLC38A5-treated HRMECs also shows a reciprocal ~25% higher levels of glutamine content than si-Ctrl-treated cells (p≤0.01, Figure 6B), suggesting effective blockade of glutamine transport into HRMECs.
evidence: Demonstrated by glutamine/glutamate bioluminescent assay measuring glutamine levels in culture medium, as shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Treatment with glutamine enhanced HRMEC proliferation in MTT assays, which was blocked by DON.
source: Treatment with glutamine enhanced HRMEC proliferation in MTT assays, which was blocked by a glutamine antagonist 6-diazo-5-oxo-L-norleucine (DON) (Figure 6D).
evidence: Demonstrated by MTT cell viability assay showing increased cell growth with glutamine treatment and reversal by DON, as shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Glutamine treatment substantially increased HRMEC migration by ~50%, which was reversed by DON treatment.
source: Moreover, glutamine treatment substantially increased HRMEC migration by ~50% (Figure 6B and E) and tubular formation by more than twofold (Figure 6C and F), both of which were reversed by DON treatment.
evidence: Demonstrated by scratch wound migration assay showing increased migration with glutamine and reversal by DON, as shown in Figure 6B and E.

claim: Glutamine treatment increased HRMEC tubular formation by more than twofold, which was reversed by DON treatment.
source: Moreover, glutamine treatment substantially increased HRMEC migration by ~50% (Figure 6B and E) and tubular formation by more than twofold (Figure 6C and F), both of which were reversed by DON treatment.
evidence: Demonstrated by tubular formation assay showing increased vessel length with glutamine and reversal by DON, as shown in Figure 6C and F.

claim: Suppression of SLC38A5 led to substantially altered mRNA expression of VEGFR1, VEGFR2, Tie2, FGFR1-3, IGF1R, IGF2R, ERK1, ERK2, and mTOR in HRMECs.
source: Suppression of SLC38A5 led to substantially altered mRNA expression of VEGF receptors (VEGFR1 and VEGFR2), Tie2, FGF receptors (FGFR1-3), IGF1R, and IGF2R (Figure 7A). In addition, there was substantial suppression of expression of ERK1 and 2 and mTOR (Figure 7A), key mediators downstream of VEGFR2 signaling that controls EC growth.
evidence: Demonstrated by RT-qPCR analysis of multiple growth factor receptors and signaling molecules in si-SLC38A5-treated HRMECs, as shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Protein levels of VEGFR1 were substantially up-regulated after SLC38A5 knockdown in HRMECs.
source: Protein levels of VEGFR1 were substantially up-regulated, whereas VEGFR2 levels were substantially suppressed after SLC38A5 knockdown in HRMECs (Figure 7B).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis showing increased VEGFR1 protein levels in si-SLC38A5-treated HRMECs, as shown in Figure 7B.

claim: VEGFR2 protein levels were substantially suppressed after SLC38A5 knockdown in HRMECs.
source: Protein levels of VEGFR1 were substantially up-regulated, whereas VEGFR2 levels were substantially suppressed after SLC38A5 knockdown in HRMECs (Figure 7B).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis showing decreased VEGFR2 protein levels in si-SLC38A5-treated HRMECs, as shown in Figure 7B.

claim: SLC38A5 is an amino acid transporter that shuttles neutral AAs across cell membrane, including glutamine.
source: SLC38A5 (solute carrier family 38 member 5), an AA transporter, shuttles neutral AAs across cell membrane, including glutamine, which may serve as metabolic fuel for proliferating endothelial cells (ECs) to promote angiogenesis.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of SLC38A5 function as documented in the literature.

claim: Glutamine may serve as metabolic fuel for proliferating endothelial cells to promote angiogenesis.
source: SLC38A5 (solute carrier family 38 member 5), an AA transporter, shuttles neutral AAs across cell membrane, including glutamine, which may serve as metabolic fuel for proliferating endothelial cells (ECs) to promote angiogenesis.
evidence: Based on established knowledge from the literature about glutamine's role in EC metabolism and angiogenesis.

claim: Slc38a5 is highly enriched in normal retinal vascular endothelium.
source: Here, we found that Slc38a5 is highly enriched in normal retinal vascular endothelium, and more specifically, in pathological sprouting neovessels.
evidence: Supported by laser capture microdissection data showing ~40-fold enrichment in retinal blood vessels and single-cell transcriptome analysis.

claim: Slc38a5 is highly enriched in pathological sprouting neovessels.
source: Here, we found that Slc38a5 is highly enriched in normal retinal vascular endothelium, and more specifically, in pathological sprouting neovessels.
evidence: Supported by data showing ~2.5-fold enrichment in OIR pathological neovessels compared to normal vessels.

claim: Slc38a5 is suppressed in retinal blood vessels from Lrp5−/− mice.
source: Slc38a5 is suppressed in retinal blood vessels from Lrp5−/− and Ndpy/− mice, both genetic models of defective retinal vascular development with Wnt signaling mutations.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR and Western blot data showing decreased Slc38a5 expression in Lrp5−/− retinas and vessels.

claim: Slc38a5 is suppressed in retinal blood vessels from Ndpy/− mice.
source: Slc38a5 is suppressed in retinal blood vessels from Lrp5−/− and Ndpy/− mice, both genetic models of defective retinal vascular development with Wnt signaling mutations.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR and Western blot data showing decreased Slc38a5 expression in Ndpy/− retinas and vessels.

claim: Lrp5−/− and Ndpy/− mice are genetic models of defective retinal vascular development with Wnt signaling mutations.
source: Slc38a5 is suppressed in retinal blood vessels from Lrp5−/− and Ndpy/− mice, both genetic models of defective retinal vascular development with Wnt signaling mutations.
evidence: Based on established knowledge from the literature about these mouse models and their Wnt signaling defects.

claim: Slc38a5 transcription is regulated by Wnt/β-catenin signaling.
source: Additionally, Slc38a5 transcription is regulated by Wnt/β-catenin signaling.
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assays showing β-catenin-dependent activation of SLC38A5 promoter regions and Wnt ligand treatment experiments.

claim: Genetic deficiency of Slc38a5 in mice substantially delays retinal vascular development.
source: Genetic deficiency of Slc38a5 in mice substantially delays retinal vascular development and suppresses pathological neovascularization in oxygen-induced retinopathy modeling ischemic proliferative retinopathies.
evidence: Supported by quantification of vascular coverage in Slc38a5−/− retinas at P5 and P10 showing delayed development.

claim: Genetic deficiency of Slc38a5 in mice suppresses pathological neovascularization in oxygen-induced retinopathy.
source: Genetic deficiency of Slc38a5 in mice substantially delays retinal vascular development and suppresses pathological neovascularization in oxygen-induced retinopathy modeling ischemic proliferative retinopathies.
evidence: Supported by quantification showing ~25% reduction in pathological neovascularization in Slc38a5−/− OIR retinas.

claim: Inhibition of SLC38A5 in human retinal vascular ECs impairs EC proliferation.
source: Inhibition of SLC38A5 in human retinal vascular ECs impairs EC proliferation and angiogenic function, suppresses glutamine uptake, and dampens vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2.
evidence: Supported by MTT assay showing ~30% reduction in HRMEC metabolic activity at 72 hr after si-SLC38A5 treatment.

claim: Inhibition of SLC38A5 in human retinal vascular ECs impairs EC angiogenic function.
source: Inhibition of SLC38A5 in human retinal vascular ECs impairs EC proliferation and angiogenic function, suppresses glutamine uptake, and dampens vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2.
evidence: Supported by migration and tubular formation assays showing reduced angiogenic capacity in si-SLC38A5-treated HRMECs.

claim: Inhibition of SLC38A5 in human retinal vascular ECs suppresses glutamine uptake.
source: Inhibition of SLC38A5 in human retinal vascular ECs impairs EC proliferation and angiogenic function, suppresses glutamine uptake, and dampens vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2.
evidence: Supported by glutamine/glutamate bioluminescent assay showing ~25% decrease in intracellular glutamine and ~25% increase in medium glutamine.

claim: Inhibition of SLC38A5 in human retinal vascular ECs dampens vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2.
source: Inhibition of SLC38A5 in human retinal vascular ECs impairs EC proliferation and angiogenic function, suppresses glutamine uptake, and dampens vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2.
evidence: Supported by Western blot showing substantially suppressed VEGFR2 protein levels after SLC38A5 knockdown.

claim: SLC38A5 is a new metabolic regulator of retinal angiogenesis by controlling AA nutrient uptake and homeostasis in ECs.
source: Together these findings suggest that SLC38A5 is a new metabolic regulator of retinal angiogenesis by controlling AA nutrient uptake and homeostasis in ECs.
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of evidence including glutamine uptake assays, angiogenic function assays, and in vivo vascular development studies.

claim: Angiogenesis is the growth of new blood vessels from existing vessels.
source: Angiogenesis, the growth of new blood vessels from existing vessels, is important in both development and disease (Folkman, 1995).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge and supported by citation to Folkman, 1995.

claim: Formation of blood vessels in the developing eye allows delivery of nutrients and removal of metabolic waste from neuronal retinas.
source: In the developing eye, formation of blood vessels allows delivery of nutrients and removal of metabolic waste from neuronal retinas (Selvam et al., 2018; Stahl et al., 2010).
evidence: Based on established knowledge supported by citations to Selvam et al., 2018 and Stahl et al., 2010.

claim: In proliferative retinopathies, abnormal proliferation of pathological blood vessels may lead to retinal detachment and vision loss.
source: In vascular eye diseases, specifically proliferative retinopathies, such as retinopathy of prematurity and diabetic retinopathy, abnormal proliferation of pathological blood vessels may lead to retinal detachment and vision loss (Chen and Smith, 2007; Hartnett and Penn, 2012; Antonetti et al., 2012).
evidence: Based on established clinical knowledge supported by citations to Chen and Smith, 2007; Hartnett and Penn, 2012; Antonetti et al., 2012.

claim: Metabolism in vascular endothelial cells has been recognized as a driving force of angiogenesis.
source: In addition to growth factors, metabolism in vascular endothelial cells (ECs) has been recognized as a driving force of angiogenesis (Rohlenova et al., 2018; De Bock et al., 2013a).
evidence: Based on established knowledge from recent literature supported by citations to Rohlenova et al., 2018 and De Bock et al., 2013a.

claim: Both glucose glycolysis and fatty acid oxidation play major roles in regulating angiogenesis.
source: Both glucose glycolysis (De Bock et al., 2013b; Yu et al., 2017; Wilhelm et al., 2016) and fatty acid oxidation (Vander Heiden et al., 2009; Neely and Morgan, 1974; Saddik and Lopaschuk, 1994; Kuo et al., 2017) play major roles in regulating angiogenesis, and more specifically in ocular angiogenesis (Joyal et al., 2017; Fu et al., 2017; Smith and Connor, 2005).
evidence: Based on established knowledge from literature supported by multiple citations.

claim: Metabolism of amino acids such as glutamine is increasingly established as an essential energy source in EC sprouting and angiogenesis.
source: Moreover, metabolism of amino acids (AAs), such as glutamine, is increasingly established as an essential energy source in EC sprouting and angiogenesis (Rohlenova et al., 2018; Dang, 2012).
evidence: Based on recent literature supported by citations to Rohlenova et al., 2018 and Dang, 2012.

claim: Glutamine is the most abundant non-essential AA in the body.
source: Glutamine, the most abundant non-essential AA in the body, is a key carbon and nitrogen source and can be metabolized to sustain EC growth (Huang et al., 2017; DeBerardinis and Cheng, 2010).
evidence: Based on established biochemical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Glutamine can act as an anaplerotic source of carbon to replenish the tricarboxylic acid cycle and support protein and nucleotide synthesis in EC growth.
source: It can act as an anaplerotic source of carbon to replenish the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle and support protein and nucleotide synthesis in EC growth (Huang et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2017a).
evidence: Based on established metabolic knowledge supported by citations to Huang et al., 2017 and Kim et al., 2017a.

claim: Glutamine deprivation severely impairs EC proliferation and vessel sprouting.
source: Glutamine deprivation severely impairs EC proliferation and vessel sprouting, and pharmacological blockade of glutaminase 1, an enzyme that converts glutamine to glutamate, inhibits pathological angiogenesis (Huang et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on published experimental findings supported by citation to Huang et al., 2017.

claim: Pharmacological blockade of glutaminase 1 inhibits pathological angiogenesis.
source: Glutamine deprivation severely impairs EC proliferation and vessel sprouting, and pharmacological blockade of glutaminase 1, an enzyme that converts glutamine to glutamate, inhibits pathological angiogenesis (Huang et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on published experimental findings supported by citation to Huang et al., 2017.

claim: SLC38A5 transports neutral AAs across cell membrane, including glutamine, asparagine, histidine, serine, alanine, and glycine.
source: Solute carrier family 38 member 5 (SLC38A5, also known as SNAT5: system N sodium-coupled AA transporter 5) transports neutral AAs across cell membrane, including glutamine, asparagine, histidine, serine, alanine, and glycine (Nakanishi et al., 2001).
evidence: Based on established knowledge about SLC38A5 function supported by citation to Nakanishi et al., 2001.

claim: SLC38A5 was found to mediate transcellular transport of AAs in brain glial cells.
source: Previously, SLC38A5 was found to mediate transcellular transport of AAs in brain glial cells (Cubelos et al., 2005).
evidence: Based on published findings supported by citation to Cubelos et al., 2005.

claim: SLC38A5 is a recently identified marker for pancreatic progenitors.
source: SLC38A5 is also a recently identified marker for pancreatic progenitors (Stanescu et al., 2017), where it is important for L-glutamine-dependent nutrient sensing and pancreatic alpha cell proliferation and hyperplasia (Dean et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2017b).
evidence: Based on published findings supported by citation to Stanescu et al., 2017.

claim: SLC38A5 is important for L-glutamine-dependent nutrient sensing and pancreatic alpha cell proliferation and hyperplasia.
source: SLC38A5 is also a recently identified marker for pancreatic progenitors (Stanescu et al., 2017), where it is important for L-glutamine-dependent nutrient sensing and pancreatic alpha cell proliferation and hyperplasia (Dean et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2017b).
evidence: Based on published findings supported by citations to Dean et al., 2017 and Kim et al., 2017b.

claim: SLC38A5 was previously found in Müller glial cells and retinal ganglion cells.
source: In the eye, SLC38A5 was previously found in Müller glial cells and retinal ganglion cells (Umapathy et al., 2005; Umapathy et al., 2008), yet its localization and function in other retinal cells, including vascular ECs, are less clear.
evidence: Based on published findings supported by citations to Umapathy et al., 2005 and Umapathy et al., 2008.

claim: Slc38a5 was drastically down-regulated in both Lrp5−/− and Ndpy/− retinas.
source: We and others previously found that Slc38a5 was drastically down-regulated in both Lrp5−/− and Ndpy/− retinas (Chen et al., 2012; Xia et al., 2010; Schäfer et al., 2009), experimental models of two genetic vascular eye diseases: familial exudative vitreoretinopathy (FEVR) and Norrie disease, respectively.
evidence: Based on previous findings from the authors and others supported by citations to Chen et al., 2012; Xia et al., 2010; Schäfer et al., 2009.

claim: Lrp5−/− and Ndpy/− mice are experimental models of familial exudative vitreoretinopathy (FEVR) and Norrie disease, respectively.
source: We and others previously found that Slc38a5 was drastically down-regulated in both Lrp5−/− and Ndpy/− retinas (Chen et al., 2012; Xia et al., 2010; Schäfer et al., 2009), experimental models of two genetic vascular eye diseases: familial exudative vitreoretinopathy (FEVR) and Norrie disease, respectively.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about these mouse models.

claim: Both FEVR and Norrie disease models have genetic mutations in Wnt signaling and share similar retinal vascular defects.
source: Both disease models have genetic mutations in Wnt signaling and share similar retinal vascular defects including initial incomplete or delayed vascular development, absence of deep retinal vascular layer, followed by a secondary hypoxia-driven increase in VEGF in the retina, and tuft-like neovascularization in the superficial layer of the retinal vasculature (Ye et al., 2010; Benson, 1995; Wang et al., 2016; Andersen and Warburg, 1961).
evidence: Based on established knowledge about these disease models supported by multiple citations.

claim: Slc38a5 is down-regulated 7–10-fold in Lrp5−/− retinas and Ndpy/− retinas during development.
source: Slc38a5 is down-regulated 7–10-fold in Lrp5−/− retinas and Ndpy/− retinas during development (Chen et al., 2012; Schäfer et al., 2009), indicating a potential strong connection of Slc38a5 with retinal blood vessel formation.
evidence: Based on previous findings supported by citations to Chen et al., 2012 and Schäfer et al., 2009.

claim: XAV939 is a small molecule inhibitor of the Wnt signaling pathway that works through binding to tankyrase and stabilizing the Axin proteins.
source: XAV939 is a small molecule inhibitor of the Wnt signaling pathway, and it works through binding to tankyrase and stabilizing the Axin proteins, thus increasing degradation of β-catenin and blocking Wnt signaling (Afifi et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on established knowledge about XAV939 mechanism supported by citation to Afifi et al., 2014.

claim: XAV939 increases degradation of β-catenin and blocks Wnt signaling.
source: XAV939 is a small molecule inhibitor of the Wnt signaling pathway, and it works through binding to tankyrase and stabilizing the Axin proteins, thus increasing degradation of β-catenin and blocking Wnt signaling (Afifi et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on established knowledge about XAV939 mechanism supported by citation to Afifi et al., 2014.

claim: Canonical Wnt signaling mediates transcription of its target genes through recognizing β-catenin-responsive TCF-binding motifs (A/TA/TCAAAG) on their regulatory regions.
source: Canonical Wnt signaling mediates transcription of its target genes through recognizing β-catenin-responsive TCF-binding motifs (A/TA/TCAAAG) on their regulatory regions (Oosterwegel et al., 1991).
evidence: Based on established knowledge about Wnt signaling mechanism supported by citation to Oosterwegel et al., 1991.

claim: Mice with targeted disruption of the Slc38a5 gene are grossly normal yet have decreased pancreatic alpha cell hyperplasia induced by glucagon receptor inhibition.
source: Mice with targeted disruption of the Slc38a5 gene are grossly normal yet have decreased pancreatic alpha cell hyperplasia induced by glucagon receptor inhibition (Kim et al., 2017b).
evidence: Based on published characterization of Slc38a5 knockout mice supported by citation to Kim et al., 2017b.

claim: The OIR model mimics the hypoxia-induced proliferative phase as seen in retinopathy of prematurity and diabetic retinopathy.
source: To evaluate the role of Slc38a5 in pathological retinal angiogenesis, we used a well-established OIR model (Smith et al., 1994), mimicking the hypoxia-induced proliferative phase as seen in retinopathy of prematurity and diabetic retinopathy.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about the OIR model supported by citation to Smith et al., 1994.

claim: In the OIR model, neonatal mice exposed to 75 ± 2% oxygen from P7 to P12 develop vaso-obliteration, followed by relative hypoxia that induces vaso-proliferation with maximal neovessel formation at P17.
source: In this model, neonatal mice and their nursing mother were exposed to 75 ± 2% oxygen from P7 to P12 to induce vaso-obliteration, followed by return to room air, when relative hypoxia induces vaso-proliferation with maximal neovessel formation observable at P17.
evidence: Based on established OIR protocol description.

claim: DON has structural similarity with glutamine and can lead to competitive binding of glutamine-binding proteins and their irreversible inhibition.
source: DON has structural similarity with glutamine, and hence, can lead to competitive binding of glutamine-binding proteins and their irreversible inhibition by forming a covalent adduct (Lemberg et al., 2018).
evidence: Based on established knowledge about DON mechanism supported by citation to Lemberg et al., 2018.

claim: VEGFR1 often acts as a VEGF decoy trap to modulate VEGFR2 function.
source: As VEGF-A is one of main angiogenic growth factors, we measured the protein levels of VEGF receptors including VEGFR2, the major angiogenic receptor for VEGF-A, and VEGFR1, often acting as a VEGF decoy trap to modulate VEGFR2 function (Rahimi, 2006).
evidence: Based on established knowledge about VEGFR1 function supported by citation to Rahimi, 2006.

claim: VEGFR2 is the major angiogenic receptor for VEGF-A.
source: As VEGF-A is one of main angiogenic growth factors, we measured the protein levels of VEGF receptors including VEGFR2, the major angiogenic receptor for VEGF-A, and VEGFR1, often acting as a VEGF decoy trap to modulate VEGFR2 function (Rahimi, 2006).
evidence: Based on established knowledge about VEGFR2 function.

claim: Suppression of SLC38A5 dampens EC glutamine uptake and subsequently leads to altered expression of growth factor receptors such as VEGFR1 and 2 to restrict EC angiogenesis.
source: These findings suggest that suppression of SLC38A5 dampens EC glutamine uptake, and subsequently, leads to altered expression of growth factor receptors such as VEGFR1 and 2 to restrict EC angiogenesis.
evidence: Inferred from combined data showing decreased glutamine uptake and altered VEGFR expression after SLC38A5 knockdown.

claim: SLC38A5 is a new pro-angiogenic regulator in the retinal vascular endothelium both during development and in retinopathy.
source: This study establishes that AA transporter SLC38A5 is a new pro-angiogenic regulator in the retinal vascular endothelium both during development and in retinopathy.
evidence: Concluded from multiple lines of evidence including developmental delay in Slc38a5−/− mice and reduced pathological neovascularization in OIR.

claim: Wnt signaling is fundamentally important in retinal angiogenesis.
source: SLC38A5 transcription is regulated by Wnt signaling, a fundamentally important pathway in retinal angiogenesis (Ye et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2019a).
evidence: Based on established knowledge supported by citations to Ye et al., 2010 and Wang et al., 2019a.

claim: SLC38A5 regulates retinal angiogenesis through modulating vascular EC uptake of AAs such as glutamine and thereby influencing angiogenic receptor signaling including VEGFR2 to impact EC growth and function.
source: Based on these findings, we suggest that SLC38A5 regulates retinal angiogenesis through modulating vascular EC uptake of AAs such as glutamine and thereby influencing angiogenic receptor signaling including VEGFR2 to impact EC growth and function (Figure 8).
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on integration of multiple experimental findings including glutamine uptake, VEGFR2 expression, and angiogenic function assays.

claim: Slc38a5−/− retinas do not reproduce FEVR-like symptoms as seen in Lrp5−/− and Ndpy/− mice.
source: Delayed development of Slc38a5−/− retinal vessels, however, is resolved by adult age with normal vasculature and intact deep layer of vessels (Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2), indicating that Slc38a5−/− retinas do not reproduce FEVR-like symptoms as seen in Lrp5−/− and Ndpy/− mice.
evidence: Inferred from observation that adult Slc38a5−/− mice have normal retinal vasculature unlike the persistent defects in Lrp5−/− and Ndpy/− mice.

claim: Down-regulation of Slc38a5 may only partially explain the effects of Wnt signaling on angiogenesis.
source: This suggests that down-regulation of Slc38a5 may only partially explain the effects of Wnt signaling on angiogenesis, and other Wnt- and β-catenin-mediated factors are still at work to drive defective angiogenesis in Lrp5−/− and Ndpy/− retinas, including, for example, Sox family proteins (Ye et al., 2009) and integrin-linked kinase (Park et al., 2019).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Slc38a5−/− mice have milder phenotype than Lrp5−/− and Ndpy/− mice, suggesting additional Wnt targets are involved.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin signaling is critical to maintain blood vessel barrier and prevent vascular leakage in the brain and eyes.
source: In addition to regulating retinal vessel growth, Wnt/β-catenin signaling is critical to maintain blood vessel barrier and prevent vascular leakage in the brain and eyes (Ye et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2019a; Ben and Liebner, 2022; Wang et al., 2019b).
evidence: Based on established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Slc38a5−/− eyes exhibit normal blood-retinal barrier with no detectable vascular leakage.
source: Slc38a5−/− eyes exhibit normal blood-retinal barrier with no detectable vascular leakage in fundus fluorescent imaging (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting that SLC38A5 is dispensable in mediating the effects of Wnt signaling on the retinal vascular barrier largely through both tight junctions such as claudin 5 (Chen et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2011) and regulation of EC transcytosis (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: Demonstrated by fundus fluorescein angiography showing no leakage in Slc38a5−/− eyes, as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: SLC38A5 is dispensable in mediating the effects of Wnt signaling on the retinal vascular barrier.
source: Slc38a5−/− eyes exhibit normal blood-retinal barrier with no detectable vascular leakage in fundus fluorescent imaging (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting that SLC38A5 is dispensable in mediating the effects of Wnt signaling on the retinal vascular barrier largely through both tight junctions such as claudin 5 (Chen et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2011) and regulation of EC transcytosis (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: Inferred from observation that Slc38a5−/− mice have normal vascular barrier despite Wnt regulation of SLC38A5.

claim: Slc38a5 may potentially be responsive to oxygen sensing and regulated by hypoxia/HIF.
source: Other than Wnt signaling, Slc38a5 may potentially be responsive to oxygen sensing and regulated by hypoxia/HIF (hypoxia-inducible factor), as Slc38a5 expression is suppressed in the phase I of OIR during oxygen exposure and upregulated in the second phase of relative hypoxia.
evidence: Speculated based on observed pattern of Slc38a5 expression changes during different oxygen conditions in OIR model.

claim: Wnt signaling may regulate Slc38a5 transcription indirectly through a secondary mechanism such as hypoxia through crosstalk with HIF pathway.
source: Therefore Wnt signaling may also regulate Slc38a5 transcription indirectly through a secondary mechanism such as hypoxia through crosstalk with HIF pathway.
evidence: Speculated based on observed oxygen-dependent expression patterns and known pathway interactions.

claim: Glutamine uptake in vascular endothelium is substantially down-regulated when SLC38A5 is suppressed.
source: Our data showed that glutamine uptake in vascular endothelium is substantially down-regulated when SLC38A5 is suppressed, suggesting that SLC38A5 may regulate glutamine availability to ECs and thus control EC angiogenesis and metabolism.
evidence: Demonstrated by glutamine/glutamate bioluminescent assay showing decreased intracellular and increased extracellular glutamine with SLC38A5 knockdown.

claim: SLC38A5 may regulate glutamine availability to ECs and thus control EC angiogenesis and metabolism.
source: Our data showed that glutamine uptake in vascular endothelium is substantially down-regulated when SLC38A5 is suppressed, suggesting that SLC38A5 may regulate glutamine availability to ECs and thus control EC angiogenesis and metabolism.
evidence: Inferred from combined data showing decreased glutamine uptake and impaired angiogenic function with SLC38A5 suppression.

claim: Glutamine was reported previously to fuel EC proliferation but not migration in HUVEC in vitro.
source: Glutamine was reported previously to fuel EC proliferation but not migration in HUVEC (human umbilical vein endothelial cells) in vitro (Kim et al., 2017a), yet in our study we found glutamine promotes migration of HRMECs, which may reflect different cell-specific responses to glutamine in macrovascular HUVECs vs. microvascular HRMECs, as well as different migration assay methods used.
evidence: Based on published findings supported by citation to Kim et al., 2017a, contrasted with current study findings.

claim: Glutamine promotes migration of HRMECs.
source: Glutamine was reported previously to fuel EC proliferation but not migration in HUVEC (human umbilical vein endothelial cells) in vitro (Kim et al., 2017a), yet in our study we found glutamine promotes migration of HRMECs, which may reflect different cell-specific responses to glutamine in macrovascular HUVECs vs. microvascular HRMECs, as well as different migration assay methods used.
evidence: Demonstrated by scratch wound migration assay showing increased migration with glutamine treatment in HRMECs.

claim: Different cell-specific responses to glutamine may exist between macrovascular HUVECs and microvascular HRMECs.
source: Glutamine was reported previously to fuel EC proliferation but not migration in HUVEC (human umbilical vein endothelial cells) in vitro (Kim et al., 2017a), yet in our study we found glutamine promotes migration of HRMECs, which may reflect different cell-specific responses to glutamine in macrovascular HUVECs vs. microvascular HRMECs, as well as different migration assay methods used.
evidence: Speculated to explain discrepancy between current findings and previous literature.

claim: Müller glia provide glutamine locally in the retina through uptake of and synthesis from excess extracellular glutamate as neurotransmitter.
source: While glutamine is the most abundant AA in circulation, Müller glia also provide glutamine locally in the retina through uptake of and synthesis from excess extracellular glutamate as neurotransmitter (Bringmann et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on established knowledge about Müller glia function supported by citation to Bringmann et al., 2013.

claim: SLC38A5 may help vascular ECs to uptake and utilize free glutamine from both systemic circulation and those released by Müller glia.
source: Thus SLC38A5 may help vascular ECs to uptake and utilize free glutamine from both systemic circulation and those released by Müller glia to influence AA uptake and metabolism.
evidence: Inferred from knowledge of glutamine sources and SLC38A5 transporter function.

claim: Hyperoxia promotes glutamine consumption and glutamine-fueled anaplerosis in Müller glia.
source: A recent study found that hyperoxia promotes glutamine consumption and glutamine-fueled anaplerosis in Müller glia (Singh et al., 2020), suggesting a link between oxygen sensing and glutamine metabolism in the Müller glia.
evidence: Based on published findings supported by citation to Singh et al., 2020.

claim: Serine deprivation in the absence of phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase causes lethal vascular defects in mice.
source: For example, serine deprivation in the absence of a synthesizing enzyme phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase causes lethal vascular defects in mice (Vandekeere et al., 2018), whereas serine-glycine metabolism is also required in angiogenesis and linked to endothelial dysfunction in response to oxidized phospholipids (Hitzel et al., 2018).
evidence: Based on published findings supported by citation to Vandekeere et al., 2018.

claim: Serine-glycine metabolism is required in angiogenesis and linked to endothelial dysfunction in response to oxidized phospholipids.
source: For example, serine deprivation in the absence of a synthesizing enzyme phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase causes lethal vascular defects in mice (Vandekeere et al., 2018), whereas serine-glycine metabolism is also required in angiogenesis and linked to endothelial dysfunction in response to oxidized phospholipids (Hitzel et al., 2018).
evidence: Based on published findings supported by citation to Hitzel et al., 2018.

claim: In the mouse model of OIR, serine and one-carbon metabolism mediate HIF response in retinopathy through liver-eye serine crosstalk.
source: In the mouse model of OIR, serine and one-carbon metabolism were found to mediate HIF response in retinopathy through liver-eye serine crosstalk (Singh et al., 2019).
evidence: Based on published findings supported by citation to Singh et al., 2019.

claim: In macular telangiectasia type 2, defective serine biosynthesis and PHDGH haploinsufficiency was genetically linked with disease onset.
source: In macular telangiectasia type 2 (MacTel), a rare degenerative eye disease with abnormal intraretinal angiogenesis, defective serine biosynthesis, and PHDGH haploinsufficiency was genetically linked with disease onset and associated with toxic ceramide accumulation in circulation and in retinal pigment epithelium cells (Eade et al., 2021; Gantner et al., 2019).
evidence: Based on published findings supported by citations to Eade et al., 2021 and Gantner et al., 2019.

claim: Defective serine biosynthesis in MacTel is associated with toxic ceramide accumulation in circulation and in retinal pigment epithelium cells.
source: In macular telangiectasia type 2 (MacTel), a rare degenerative eye disease with abnormal intraretinal angiogenesis, defective serine biosynthesis, and PHDGH haploinsufficiency was genetically linked with disease onset and associated with toxic ceramide accumulation in circulation and in retinal pigment epithelium cells (Eade et al., 2021; Gantner et al., 2019).
evidence: Based on published findings supported by citations to Eade et al., 2021 and Gantner et al., 2019.

claim: Decreased glutamine uptake in EC is directly associated with altered expression of growth factor receptors and particularly increased levels of VEGFR1 and decreased levels of VEGFR2.
source: We showed here that decreased glutamine uptake in EC is directly associated with altered expression of growth factor receptors and particularly increased levels of VEGFR1 and decreased levels of VEGFR2.
evidence: Demonstrated by combined data from glutamine uptake assays and Western blot analysis of VEGFR1 and VEGFR2 after SLC38A5 knockdown.

claim: Suppression of SLC38A5 may not only directly decrease VEGFR2 expression but also limit VEGFR2 function due to increased VEGFR1 levels.
source: Suppression of SLC38A5 may thus not only directly decrease VEGFR2 expression but also limit VEGFR2 function due to increased VEGFR1 levels, both of which can result in decreased retinal angiogenesis.
evidence: Inferred from data showing opposite changes in VEGFR1 and VEGFR2 levels and knowledge of VEGFR1 as a decoy receptor.

claim: Modulation of SLC38A5 and its associated AAs may have translational value in treating retinopathy.
source: Findings presented here suggest that modulation of SLC38A5 and its associated AAs may have translational value in treating retinopathy.
evidence: Speculated based on study findings showing SLC38A5's role in pathological neovascularization.

claim: Premature infants often lack conditionally essential AAs such as glutamine or arginine due to their impaired endogenous synthesis.
source: Premature infants often lack conditionally essential AAs such as glutamine or arginine (Neu, 2003; Wu et al., 2004) due to their impaired endogenous synthesis.
evidence: Based on established clinical knowledge supported by citations to Neu, 2003 and Wu et al., 2004.

claim: Providing AAs early on might promote normalization of delayed vessel growth and prevent the neovascular phase of retinopathy.
source: Providing much needed AAs early on might promote normalization of delayed vessel growth, and thereby preventing the neovascular phase of retinopathy.
evidence: Speculated based on understanding of AA role in vascular development and retinopathy pathophysiology.

claim: Supplement of an arginine-glutamine dipeptide was found to dampen pathological neovascularization in OIR by promoting normal vascular restoration.
source: Previously, supplement of an arginine-glutamine (Arg-Glu) dipeptide was found to dampen pathological neovascularization in OIR by promoting normal vascular restoration (Shaw et al., 2018; Neu et al., 2006).
evidence: Based on published findings supported by citations to Shaw et al., 2018 and Neu et al., 2006.

claim: Lack of SLC38A5 and likely subsequent impaired glutamine uptake dampens developmental angiogenesis.
source: Here our data suggest lack of SLC38A5, and likely subsequent impaired glutamine uptake, dampens developmental angiogenesis, in line with the pro-angiogenic role of AAs in the first phase of retinopathy.
evidence: Inferred from data showing delayed vascular development in Slc38a5−/− mice and decreased glutamine uptake with SLC38A5 knockdown.

claim: In the late proliferative phase of retinopathy, inhibiting AA transporters like SLC38A5 or starving retinal vessels from AA nutrients may be beneficial in suppressing pathological neovascularization.
source: In the late proliferative phase of retinopathy, however, inhibiting AA transporters like SLC38A5 or starving retinal vessels from AA nutrients may be beneficial in directly suppressing uncontrolled pathological neovascularization.
evidence: Speculated based on data showing reduced pathological neovascularization in Slc38a5−/− OIR mice.

claim: Targeting of AAs and their transporters such as SLC38A5 may represent a new potential approach to treat retinopathy via modulating EC AA transport and metabolism.
source: Targeting of AAs and their transporters such as SLC38A5 may thus represent a new potential approach to treat retinopathy via modulating EC AA transport and metabolism.
evidence: Speculated based on overall study findings showing SLC38A5's role in both developmental and pathological angiogenesis.

claim: Local inhibition of SLC38A5 directly impairs retinal angiogenesis.
source: Yet our data from ocular siRNA delivery strongly suggest that local inhibition of SLC38A5 did directly impair retinal angiogenesis, and systemic influence from other organs is likely minimal.
evidence: Demonstrated by intravitreal siRNA injection experiments showing delayed vascular development.

claim: SLC38A5 has an EC-specific pro-angiogenic role via regulating cellular AA availability and metabolism.
source: It is also not clear whether other retinal cell types, including glia and neurons may be impacted by SLC38A5 modulation and thus affect vascular endothelium metabolism and angiogenesis, although our cell culture data largely supports an EC-specific pro-angiogenic role of SLC38A5 via regulating cellular AA availability and metabolism.
evidence: Supported by in vitro HRMEC experiments showing direct effects on EC function, though acknowledging potential indirect effects from other cell types.

claim: SLC38A5 is a novel regulator of EC AA metabolism and retinal angiogenesis.
source: In summary, our data present direct evidence that SLC38A5 is a novel regulator of EC AA metabolism and retinal angiogenesis.
evidence: Concluded from comprehensive data including expression studies, functional assays, and in vivo models.

claim: Expression of SLC38A5 is enriched in sprouting neovessels and driven by Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway.
source: Expression of SLC38A5 is enriched in sprouting neovessels and driven by Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway, as evident in Wnt-deficient retinas.
evidence: Supported by data showing enrichment in OIR neovessels, down-regulation in Wnt-deficient mice, and luciferase reporter assays.

claim: Suppression of SLC38A5 may limit glutamine uptake by ECs, resulting in altered cellular metabolism, dampened VEGFR2 signaling and blunted retinal angiogenesis.
source: Suppression of SLC38A5 may limit glutamine uptake by ECs, resulting in altered cellular metabolism, dampened VEGFR2 signaling and blunted retinal angiogenesis.
evidence: Inferred from combined data showing decreased glutamine uptake, reduced VEGFR2 expression, and impaired angiogenic function with SLC38A5 suppression.

claim: SLC38A5 is a modulator of pathologic retinal angiogenesis.
source: Our findings of SLC38A5 as a modulator of pathologic retinal angiogenesis suggest the possibility of targeting SLC38A5 and its transported AAs as new therapeutic intervention for the treatment of vascular eye diseases and potentially other angiogenesis-related diseases.
evidence: Concluded from data showing reduced pathological neovascularization in Slc38a5−/− OIR mice.

claim: Targeting SLC38A5 and its transported AAs may be a new therapeutic intervention for the treatment of vascular eye diseases and potentially other angiogenesis-related diseases.
source: Our findings of SLC38A5 as a modulator of pathologic retinal angiogenesis suggest the possibility of targeting SLC38A5 and its transported AAs as new therapeutic intervention for the treatment of vascular eye diseases and potentially other angiogenesis-related diseases.
evidence: Speculated based on overall study findings demonstrating SLC38A5's role in pathological angiogenesis.
